The key component is structure-conditioned modeling, realized through Structure-Guided Feature Tokenizer (SGFT) construction and information sampling. 3.1 Structure-Guided Feature Tokenizer We construct a multi-scale extractor over the image x x by recursively partitioning its domain. However, the standard greedy selection, n ∗ = arg ⁡ max ⁡ V ⁡ ( n j ) n^{*}=\arg\max V(n_{j}) , is inherently sequential and non-parallelizable, creating a computational bottleneck as the number of active k k increases. To address this, we "soften" the selection by reformulating the splitting criteria as a probabilistic sampling process. We define a probability distribution π \pi over the set of active tokens 𝒜 k \mathcal{A}_{k} , where the probability of selecting a token n j n_{j} is proportional to its salience score. The transition from current token set 𝒜 k \mathcal{A}_{k} to next set 𝒜 k + s − 1 \mathcal{A}_{k+s-1} is defined recursively: 𝒜 k + s − 1 = { 𝒜 k , if k ≥ N ( 𝒜 k ∖ { n ∗ } ) ∪ Split ​ ( n ∗ ) , n ∗ ∼ π ( ⋅ | 𝒜 k , τ ) \displaystyle\scriptsize\mathcal{A}_{k+s-1}=\begin{cases}\mathcal{A}_{k},&\text{if $k\geq N$}\\ (\mathcal{A}_{k}\setminus\{n^{*}\})\cup\text{Split}(n^{*}),&n^{*}\sim\pi(\cdot|\mathcal{A}_{k},\tau)\end{cases} (1) where N N is the target fixed sequence length for the model. The probability distribution π \pi is defined using the softmax function with a temperature parameter τ \tau : π ⁡ ( n j | 𝒜 k , τ ) = exp ⁡ ( V ⁡ ( n j ) / τ ) ∑ n i ∈ 𝒜 k exp ⁡ ( V ⁡ ( n i ) / τ ) \displaystyle\scriptsize\pi(n_{j}|\mathcal{A}_{k},\tau)=\frac{\exp(V(n_{j})/\tau)}{\sum_{n_{i}\in\mathcal{A}_{k}}\exp(V(n_{i})/\tau)} (2) Here, V ⁡ ( n j ) V(n_{j}) is the scoring criterion (e.g. the sum of edge map values) for token n j n_{j} .

The temperature τ \tau controls the "softness" of the selection: as τ → 0 \tau\to 0 , π \pi approaches the original deterministic ‘argmax‘ selection, while as τ → ∞ \tau\to\infty , it approaches a uniform random selection. Beyond removing the sequential bottleneck, this softmax-batched formulation is also substantially faster in wall-clock terms than the SHF/AP-style arg ⁡ max \arg\max tokenizer (up to 20 × 20\times at N = 10 6 N{=}10^{6} tokens) at matched tokenization quality; we report a full per-resolution comparison in Appendix (Table ). 3.2 Structure-Guided Information Sampling We define the state of the joint process at step k k (representing a tree with k k tokens) as the tuple X k = ( 𝒜 k , C N ( k ) ) X_{k}=(\mathcal{A}_{k},C_{N}^{(k)}) , where 𝒜 k \mathcal{A}_{k} is the set of active tokens and C N ( k ) C_{N}^{(k)} is the full-resolution cumulative structure canvas. The transition X k → X k + s − 1 X_{k}\to X_{k+s-1} is defined recursively: X k + s − 1 = { X k , if k ≥ N ( 𝒜 k + s − 1 , C N ( k + s − 1 ) ) , otherwise \displaystyle\scriptsize X_{k+s-1}=\begin{cases}X_{k},&\text{if $k\geq N$}\\ (\mathcal{A}_{k+s-1},C_{N}^{(k+s-1)}),&\text{otherwise}\end{cases} (3) where N N is the target sequence length. The process is initialized at k = 1 k=1 with the root state X 1 = ( 𝒜 1 , C N ( 1 ) ) X_{1}=(\mathcal{A}_{1},C_{N}^{(1)}) . This state consists of the initial token set 𝒜 1 = { n 0 } \mathcal{A}_{1}=\{n_{0}\} , which contains only the root node n 0 n_{0} (at depth j = 0 j=0 ), and the initial structure canvas C N ( 1 ) C_{N}^{(1)} . The accumulation grows sub-linearly with depth, avoiding variance explosion. 3.3 SGMA Pre-training Framework Image Encoder and Input . After completing adaptive structural patching ( section 3.1 ) and structure-conditioned sampling distribution generation, we obtain the adaptive structural patch sequence 𝒫 = { p i } i = 1 N h \mathcal{P}=\{p_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N_{h}} and the final structure-conditioned sampling distribution N i N_{i} for each patch. We randomly select a subset of indices ℐ masked ⊂ { 1 , … , N h } \mathcal{I}_{\text{masked}}\subset\{1,\dots,N_{h}\} (e.g. 75% suggested in [ 22 ] ) to be corrupted. We then form a visible input sequence 𝒫 ′ = 𝒫 − ℐ masked \mathcal{P}^{\prime}=\mathcal{P}-\mathcal{I}_{\text{masked}} . We use a standard ViT encoder f θ f_{\theta} [ 19 ] . Following the Masked Autoencoder (MAE) paradigm, the encoder f θ f_{\theta} processes the structure-aware , clean sequence 𝒫 ′ \mathcal{P}^{\prime} . Reconstruction . A lightweight decoder g ϕ g_{\phi} is attached to the encoder f θ f_{\theta} . The decoder receives the full sequence of encoded representations Z = f θ ​ ( 𝒫 ′ ) Z=f_{\theta}(\mathcal{P}^{\prime}) and is tasked with reconstructing the original, clean version of only the noised patches . The model learns to leverage the clean patches ( p j ∈ 𝒫 ′ p_{j}{\in}\mathcal{P}^{\prime} ) as context to reconstruct corrupted patches ( i ∈ ℐ masked i{\in}\mathcal{I}_{\text{masked}} ).

This pre-training objective function ℒ SGMA \mathcal{L}_{\text{SGMA}} is: min θ , ϕ ⁡ 𝔼 I ∼ 𝒟 , ℐ masked ∼ Mask ​ [ ∑ i ∈ ℐ masked ℒ MSE ​ ( g ϕ ​ ( f θ ​ ( 𝒫 ′ ) , i ) , p i ) ] \scriptsize\min_{\theta,\phi}\;\mathbb{E}_{I\sim\mathcal{D},\,\mathcal{I}_{\text{masked}}\sim\text{Mask}}\Bigg[\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{\text{masked}}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{MSE}}\Big(g_{\phi}\big(f_{\theta}(\mathcal{P}^{\prime}),i\big),\ p_{i}\Big)\Bigg] (5) Where I I is an image from dataset 𝒟 \mathcal{D} , 𝒫 ′ \mathcal{P}^{\prime} is the corrupted input sequence, p i p_{i} is the clean patch, g ϕ ​ ( ⋅ , i ) g_{\phi}(\cdot,i) is the decoder prediction for the i i -th patch, and ℒ MSE \mathcal{L}_{\text{MSE}} is the L2 loss. 3.4 Fine-tuning Fine-tuning Encoder . After pre-training with ℒ SGMA \mathcal{L}_{\text{SGMA}} , the reconstruction decoder g ϕ g_{\phi} is discarded. We load the weights of our pre-trained encoder f θ f_{\theta} and adapt it for downstream tasks, such as segmentation. We retrofit our SGMA scheme into a segmentation framework, minimally adapting the encoder f θ f_{\theta} to process high-resolution inputs. Fine-tuning Objective . During the fine-tuning phase, we do not directly generate full-resolution masks Y Y but instead generate encoded mask logits Y ′ = { y i ′ } i = 1 N Y^{\prime}=\{y^{\prime}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} at the patch level. This saves memory and reduces backpropagation costs. To preserve structure, the target PAMPS network was interpenetrated with a PDMAAm "skeleton network". A novel mineralization technique using Fe³+ ions (forming AFO nanoparticles) provided the necessary electron contrast. The resin-substituted samples were cut into 100 nm thick specimens and observed by Hitachi and JEOL TEM/STEM systems (100-200 kV). SpringXCT-8K: A high-resolution XCT dataset of 46 concrete and asphalt specimens scanned at SPring-8 (200 keV) [ 53 ] . Each 3D volume has size 8,192 × 8,192 × 28,800 8{,}192\times 8{,}192\times 28{,}800 . For pre-training , we use 308,000 308{,}000 slices of size 8,192 × 8,192 8{,}192\times 8{,}192 . For fine-tuning , we build a simulation pipeline to generate ultrahigh-resolution data. We start from virtual microstructures [ 69 ] , resample them to 12.02 μ \mu m resolution, and obtain 1,500 1{,}500 slices of size 8,192 × 8,192 8{,}192\times 8{,}192 . We then simulate the imaging process with realistic attenuation, and add degradations such as sparse angles, Poisson/Gaussian noise, and ring artifacts. The sinograms are reconstructed using FBP [ 49 , 4 ] . This yields 60 synthetic volumes with ground-truth labels and corresponding reconstructions (see appendix) for training. PAIP-32K: [ 30 ] is a high-resolution, real-world liver cancer pathology dataset, with sample resolutions up to 64 ​ K 2 64K^{2} , significantly surpassing those of conventional image datasets. PAIP contains 2,457 2,457 Whole-Slide Images (WSIs).

When lower resolutions are needed, we downscale the images to uniform sizes of [ 16,384 , 32 , 768 , 65 , 536 ] [16,384,32,768,65,536] square pixels. For training, we randomly select 70 % 70\% of samples, 10 % 10\% for validation, and 20 % 20\% for testing. All datasets are shuffled and normalized to [ 0.0 , 1.0 ] [0.0,1.0] as input for the model. 4.2 Evaluating Models: Baselines & Proposed Baseline Models: Our primary baseline is the standard Masked AutoEncoder (MAE) [ 22 ] pre-training strategy. We evaluate this on the widely-used segmentation model SAM [ 31 ] , which uses a ViT encoder (ViT-Base, Large, or Huge) pre-trained with MAE; we refer to this configuration as MAE-SAM. We also benchmark against U-Net-style models [ 46 ] , which use a contraction-expansion path with skip connections. Our main baseline in this category is the UNETR [ 20 ] , for which we create an MAE-UNETR variant by pre-training its ViT encoder by the standard MAE objective. Proposed Models: We replace MAE pre-training with the proposed SGMA objective (Eq. 5 ) and apply it to the same architectures, yielding SGMA -SAM and SGMA -UNETR. For SAM-based models, we use symmetrical depatching [ 66 ] , eliminating the need for a heavy decoder. For SpringXCT-3D data, we apply the SAM 2 [ 44 ] encoder to 2D slices and stack the outputs for final prediction. For comparison, we include U-Net [ 46 ] (ImageNet-pretrained via timm [ 27 ] ), UNETR [ 20 ] , and Swin-UNet [ 5 ] . As shown in Table 1 , our SGMA pre-training method consistently outperforms standard baselines and MAE-based pre-trained models across all three diverse datasets. The performance improvement correlates significantly with image resolution. On the HydrogelTEM-1K dataset, the improvement is steady but modest; our FT-SGMA-UNETR achieves the top score of 75.33%, a +0.77 point increase over its corresponding FT-MAE-UNETR (74.56%). On the ultra-high resolution datasets, the advantage of SGMA becomes exceptionally pronounced. On the SpringXCT-8K dataset, our FT-SGMA-SAM model achieves a state-of-the-art Dice score of 95.68%, a massive +13.00 point improvement over the FT-MAE-SAM baseline (82.68%). This improvement is most dramatic on the PAIP-32K dataset. Here, our FT-SGMA-SAM 2 model (83.21%) surpasses the equivalent FT-MAE-SAM 2 model (66.37%) by +16.84 points. This demonstrates that while standard MAE performs poorly when handling ultra-high resolution inputs, our SGMA pre-training, which leverages adaptive structural patching, provides a far more effective representation for capturing both global context and micro-level details. Segmentation Results. Figure 2 provides a visual comparison on the HydrogelTEM-1K, SpringXCT-8K, and PAIP-32K datasets. Baselines like UNet produce blurry and incomplete boundaries. MAE-UNETR (which was forced to use large patch sizes during pre-training) fails to resolve individual structures, merging them into a single mass.

In contrast, our SGMA-UNETR, having been pre-trained on adaptive-scale patches via SGFT, successfully resolves fine, nm-scale structures, producing a segmentation mask that is crisp and topologically accurate. This demonstrates our model’s ability to learn meaningful multi-scale features. Although the main focus of the paper is ultra-high-resolution 2D imaging, the long-sequence problem also appears in 3D volumetric data; on standard 3D medical benchmarks (BTCV, KiTS19) SGMA -SAM 2 matches or marginally exceeds strong specialized baselines (Swin UNETR-V2, U-Mamba, nnFormer) on Dice while being 2.58 × 2.58\times – 7.15 × 7.15\times faster thanks to SGFT-based sequence compression (Appendix , Table ). We also report a PAIP-16K classification comparison against ViT, HIPT, and SHF-ViT, together with a Damped Accumulation ablation in Appendix (Table ). SGMA -ViT achieves the best performance in both Top-1 accuracy and Dice. The NoDA ablation further indicates that the impact of DA is task-dependent, with a marginal gain for classification ( + 0.88 +0.88 Top-1) but a notable improvement for segmentation ( + 3.00 +3.00 Dice), suggesting that DA primarily benefits dense prediction by introducing multi-scale spatial structure. 5.2 Compute Efficiency: Training and Inference The Baseline Bottleneck. Standard MAE-based models (MAE-UNETR, MAE-SAM1/2) must use a uniform grid. On a 32,768 × 32,768 32,768\times 32,768 image, even a large 32 × 32 32\times 32 patch size yields a sequence of N = ( 1024 ) 2 ≈ 1 ​ M N=(1024)^{2}\approx 1M patches, which is computationally intractable and causes Out-of-Memory (OOM) errors on any available hardware. To avoid OOM, baselines use very large patches (e.g. 128 × 128 128\times 128 or 256 × 256 256\times 256 ), losing the fine-grained details needed for our tasks. SGMA Efficiency. SGMA compresses the input into a fixed-length sequence K K (e.g. K = 1024 K=1024 or K = 4096 K=4096 ) regardless of the input resolution.

This adaptive compression allows us to process the 32K image with the same computational budget as the 1K image. As shown in Table 2 , our SGMA pre-training framework achieves a dramatic improvement in both training and inference speed compared to a MAE-based baseline (which must operate on large patches to avoid OOM). Our method is significantly faster, enabling rapid experimentation and pre-training on massive scientific datasets that were previously infeasible. Worth mentioning that, the setup of Table 2 is intentionally biased against our method on both axes. On the MAE side, the chosen sequence length is the largest the GPU budget can fit before going OOM, i.e. MAE is reported at its hardware ceiling. On the SGMA side, we deliberately use a sub-optimal short sequence (e.g. N = 2,048 N{=}2{,}048 on PAIP-32K, far below the N = 16,384 N{=}16{,}384 used by our best-Dice configuration in Table 1 ), so that compute matches and we can isolate the speedup. Even with this handicap, SGMA still beats MAE on Dice (e.g. 76.08 76.08 vs. 62.34 62.34 on PAIP-32K, a + 13.7 +13.7 -point margin). Beyond raw segmentation accuracy, we also evaluate SGMA in a zero-shot setting on real samples and use the resulting masks for downstream scientific analysis (pore-network extraction on SpringXCT-8K and hydrogel skeletonization on HydrogelTEM-1K). Using structure-guided masked autoencoders, SGMA avoids the O ⁡ ( N 2 ) O(N^{2}) bottleneck and preserves important fine-scale structures. Across TEM, XCT, and WSI datasets, SGMA achieves consistently better segmentation accuracy than MAE, including gains of +16.84% Dice on 32K pathology and up to 24.8 × 24.8\times faster inference. SGMA also enables reliable zero-shot analysis, such as pore-network extraction and hydrogel skeletonization. Model Size. A.3 Zero-shot Downstream Tasks Evaluation We use the zero-shot segmentation masks from the SpringXCT-8K and HydrogelTEM-1K datasets to conduct a statistical analysis of the components and connections. Before presenting the downstream statistics, we first visualize the per-sample segmentation quality that drives them. Figure 7 compares four segmentation models on an identical simulated SpringXCT-8K slice (ground-truth mask available): the vanilla UNet [ 46 ] collapses on small pores ( 58.38 % 58.38\% Dice), the Adaptive Patching baseline [ 65 ] at N = 8,194 N{=}8{,}194 tokens improves but still misses thin channels, the MAE-pretrained SAM 2 [ 44 ] at a 128 × 128 128{\times}128 patch is forced to operate at coarse resolution by GPU memory ( 85.98 % 85.98\% Dice), and our SGMA -SAM 2 at a 2 × 2 2{\times}2 effective patch with N = 8,194 N{=}8{,}194 SGFT tokens recovers the full pore topology ( 94.79 % 94.79\% Dice). This side-by-side view is what our Table 1 Dice gains look like at the pixel level on a single sample, and it explains why the downstream statistics in the next paragraphs are only reliable for SGMA -derived masks. As shown in Figure 8 and Figure 9 , the components derived from our SGMA-UNETR segmentations yield a near-perfect segmentation on real samples. In contrast, the statistics derived from the MAE-SAM 2 masks are noisy and unreliable, systematically underestimating the volume of small pores that its large-patch pre-training failed to capture. A.5 Comparison with Long-Sequence and Hierarchical Transformer Methods Table A.5 summarizes how SGMA compares against prior long-sequence and hierarchical Transformer methods along four axes: best-case complexity, attention mechanism invariance (i.e. whether the approach requires modifying self-attention itself), model-architecture coupling (whether the method is tied to a specific forked backbone), and implementation locus (attention kernel vs. model vs. input-preprocessing).

Most prior work either (i) approximates attention with sparsity, low-rank, or locality assumptions, which trades off accuracy for speed and often requires forked PyTorch kernels; or (ii) designs hierarchical backbones (CrossViT, HIPT, MEGABYTE) that need multiple trained models and impose specific inductive biases. In contrast, SGMA operates entirely at the input-preprocessing stage: it leaves the attention mechanism and ViT architecture untouched, and instead produces a fixed-length structure-conditioned token sequence via the Structure-Guided Feature Tokenizer (SGFT). This makes SGMA a drop-in replacement for MAE pre-training on any standard ViT, yet reduces the effective complexity to O ⁡ ( log 2 ⁡ N ) O(\log^{2}N) in the input resolution N N in the best case.
